claim: ETTIN (ETT/ARF3) is an atypical auxin response factor lacking the Aux/IAA-interacting Phox/Bem1 (PB1) domain.
source: However, ETT is an unusual ARF lacking the Aux/IAA-interacting Phox/Bem1 (PB1) domain (Simonini et al., 2016; Sessions et al., 1997) and is therefore unlikely to mediate auxin signalling via the canonical pathway.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Simonini et al., 2016; Sessions et al., 1997) that characterized ETT structure.

claim: ETT binds auxin directly as demonstrated by DARTS assay.
source: Treatments with IAA but not BA protected ETT-FLAG from pronase-induced degradation consistent with direct, specific interaction between IAA and ETT in planta.
evidence: Experimental data from DARTS assay shown in Figure 1a demonstrating differential proteolytic protection with IAA vs BA treatment.

claim: The ES domain of ETT (ES388-594) is largely intrinsically disordered but shows some propensity to form secondary structure with helical character.
source: The HSQC spectrum, recorded at 5 °C, shows a prominent signal-dense region consistent with the ES domain being largely intrinsically disordered. Interestingly, the spectrum also shows dispersed peaks flanking the signal-dense region indicating that there is nevertheless some propensity to form secondary structure, particularly with a helical character (Figure 1b).
evidence: NMR spectroscopy data showing signal distribution patterns characteristic of intrinsically disordered proteins with some structured regions.

claim: Specific residues in the ETT protein experience a changed chemical environment in response to IAA binding but not benzoic acid.
source: We found that a number of residues shifted their position in the spectrum in response to the addition of IAA, whereas addition of BA had no effect (Figure 1b–d).
evidence: HSQC-NMR experimental data showing chemical shifts upon IAA addition but not BA addition.

claim: Tryptophan W505 in ETT has a prominent role in the interaction with IAA.
source: However, a particularly large change is observed for the tryptophan NH cross peak when IAA is added to the ETT fragment (~10 ppm, rectangle I in Figure 1b,d). Since there is only one tryptophan in the ETT fragment used here (W505), this shift can be assigned to this residue and suggests that W505 has a prominent role in the interaction with IAA.
evidence: NMR data showing large chemical shift for the single tryptophan residue upon IAA addition.

claim: ETT binds IAA as demonstrated by isothermal titration calorimetry showing heat exchange between ETT and IAA.
source: This experiment revealed interaction between ETT and IAA, while control experiments titrating IAA into buffer without protein and titrating buffer without IAA into the ETT fragment showed no heat exchange (Figure 1e–g).
evidence: ITC experimental data showing heat exchange specifically when ETT and IAA are combined, but not in control conditions.

claim: PINOID (PID) and HECATE1 (HEC1) are ETT target genes that are upregulated in ett-3 mutant gynoecium tissue compared to wild type.
source: Previously, PINOID (PID) (Benjamins et al., 2001) and HECATE1 (HEC1) (Gremski et al., 2007) were identified as ETT target genes (Simonini et al., 2016; Simonini et al., 2017) and both genes are upregulated in gynoecium tissue from the ett-3 mutant compared to wild type (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Expression data from qRT-PCR comparing wild type and ett-3 mutant, supported by previous citations identifying these as ETT targets.

claim: PID and HEC1 expression is induced by IAA but shows no additional induction beyond constitutive upregulation in the ett-3 mutant background.
source: We also observed that expression of both genes is induced by IAA, but did not observe any additional induction beyond the constitutive upregulation in the ett-3 mutant background (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: qRT-PCR expression data comparing IAA-treated and untreated samples in wild type and ett-3 mutant.

claim: ETT-dependent regulation of PID and HEC1 does not require a functional TIR1/AFB machinery.
source: This ETT-dependent regulation does not require a functional TIR1/AFB machinery, since IAA-induction of PID and HEC1 is still observed in tir1/afb mutant combinations, whereas the known TIR1/AFB-mediated auxin induction of the IAA19 gene is completely abolished in these mutants (Figure 2a–c).
evidence: Expression analysis in tir1/afb mutants showing differential response of IAA19 vs PID/HEC1 to auxin treatment.

claim: IAA19 expression is upregulated in response to auxin in wild-type gynoecia but not in tir1/afb double and triple mutants.
source: IAA19 expression is up-regulated in response to auxin in wild-type gynoecia (Col-0) but not in tir1/afb double and triple mutants.
evidence: qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2a demonstrating differential IAA19 response in wild type vs tir1/afb mutants.

claim: HEC1 and PID are upregulated in response to auxin in both wild-type and auxin receptor mutants.
source: The ETT-target genes HEC1 and PID are up-regulated in response to auxin in both wild-type and auxin receptor mutants (b c). This suggests a TIR1/AFB independent regulation of these genes.
evidence: qRT-PCR data in Figure 2b,c showing auxin response in both wild type and tir1/afb mutants.

claim: PID and HEC1 expression is not significantly affected by cvxIAA in the ccvTIR1 background, but still responds to IAA.
source: In contrast, PID and HEC1 expression was not significantly affected by cvxIAA, whilst still responding to IAA in the ccvTIR1 background (Figure 2d).
evidence: Expression analysis using synthetic auxin-TIR1 pair showing differential response to cvxIAA vs IAA.

claim: IAA19 is strongly upregulated by cvxIAA in the ccvTIR1 line, but not by IAA.
source: Indeed, IAA19 was strongly upregulated by cvxIAA in the ccvTIR1 line, but not by IAA (Figure 2d).
evidence: qRT-PCR data demonstrating specific response of IAA19 to cvxIAA in engineered TIR1 system.

claim: ETT-mediated auxin signalling can occur independently of the canonical TIR1/AFB signalling pathway.
source: These data demonstrate that ETT-mediated auxin signalling can occur independently of the canonical TIR1/AFB signalling pathway.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from synthetic auxin-TIR1 pair experiments showing differential regulation of ETT targets vs canonical auxin-responsive genes.

claim: The DNA-binding domain characteristic to B3-type transcription factors such as ARF proteins is conserved across all ETT proteins in angiosperms.
source: Unsurprisingly, the DNA-binding domain characteristic to B3-type TFs such as ARF proteins was conserved across all ETT proteins.
evidence: Phylogenetic analysis of ETT protein sequences across 22 angiosperm species.

claim: An EAR-like motif with particularly high conservation is located towards the C terminus of the ES domain in ETT.
source: Towards the C terminus of the ES domain we identified an EAR-like motif with a particularly high level of conservation (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Phylogenetic analysis and sequence alignment showing conserved motif across species.

claim: ETT interacts with TPL, TPR2 and TPR4 in yeast two-hybrid assays.
source: To test this, we carried out Yeast 2-Hybrid (Y2H) assays in which ETT was found to interact with TPL, TPR2 and TPR4 (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Y2H experimental data showing protein-protein interactions.

claim: Mutating residues in the EAR-like motif abolishes ETT interactions with TPL/TPR proteins.
source: Moreover, mutating residues in the EAR-like motif abolished the interactions demonstrating its requirement for the ETT-TPL/TPR interaction (Figure 3b).
evidence: Y2H data comparing wild-type ETT and EAR-like motif mutant interactions with TPL/TPR proteins.

claim: ETT-TPL/TPR interactions are reduced with increasing IAA concentrations in both Y2H and co-immunoprecipitation experiments.
source: In both Y2H and in co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) experiments, we observed that the interactions were reduced with increasing IAA concentrations (Figure 3b,c and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Y2H and Co-IP experimental data showing dose-dependent reduction of interaction with IAA treatment.

claim: The auxin sensitivity of ETT-TPL/TPR interactions is specific to IAA as other auxinic compounds tested did not show this effect.
source: Moreover, as described previously for other ETT-protein interactions, the sensitivity was specific to IAA as other auxinic compounds tested did not show this effect (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Experimental data testing multiple auxinic compounds (BA, NAA, 2,4D) showing specificity to IAA.

claim: W505 is required for the ETT-TPL/TPR interaction to be sensitive to auxin.
source: Both Y2H and Co-IP experiments revealed that W505 is required for the ETT-TPL/TPR interaction to be sensitive to auxin (Figure 3c,d).
evidence: Y2H and Co-IP data comparing wild-type ETT and W505A mutant responses to auxin.

claim: W505 is highly conserved in ETT proteins across angiosperms.
source: The key importance of W505 is furthermore supported by a phylogenetic analysis of ETT protein sequences revealing that this residue is highly conserved in ETT proteins across angiosperms (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Phylogenetic analysis showing conservation of W505 across species.

claim: TPL and TPR2 exhibit strong expression in the apical part of the gynoecium where ETT is also expressed.
source: Both pTPL:GUS and pTPR2:GUS exhibited strong expression in the apical part of the gynoecium where ETT is also expressed, while no pTPR4:GUS expression was observed (Figure 4a–d).
evidence: GUS reporter expression data showing overlapping expression patterns.

claim: The tpl tpr2 double mutant has defects in the development of the apical gynoecium similar to ett mutants.
source: However, the tpl tpr2 double mutant has defects in the development of the apical gynoecium similar to ett mutants (Figure 4e–g) demonstrating that TPL and TPR2 function redundantly in gynoecium development.
evidence: Phenotypic analysis using scanning electron microscopy showing similar developmental defects.

claim: HDA19 is required for gynoecium development as the hda19-4 mutant has strong style defects.
source: Here, our analysis of gynoecia from the hda19-4 mutant demonstrate that HDA19 is also required for gynoecium development as the hda19-4 mutant has strong style defects (Figure 4h).
evidence: Phenotypic analysis of hda19-4 mutant showing developmental defects.

claim: HDA19 gene is highly expressed in gynoecium tissue, whereas HDA6 is not.
source: In agreement with this, the HDA19 gene was highly expressed in gynoecium tissue, whereas another member of the HDA gene family, HDA6, was not (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: qRT-PCR expression data comparing HDA19 and HDA6 expression levels in gynoecium.

claim: Expression of the ETT target genes PID and HEC1 is increased in the tpl tpr2 and hda19-4 mutants compared to wild type.
source: Moreover, HDA19 recruitment likely involves ETT, since expression of the ETT target genes, PID and HEC1, is increased in the tpl tpr2 and hda19-4 mutants compared to wild type.
evidence: qRT-PCR expression data comparing mutants to wild type.

claim: Auxin treatments fail to further induce PID and HEC1 expression in tpl tpr2 and hda19-4 mutants, similar to the ett mutant.
source: Similar to the ett mutant, auxin treatments failed to further induce expression in these mutants (Figure 4i,j).
evidence: qRT-PCR data showing lack of auxin response in mutant backgrounds.

claim: ETT, TPL and HDA19 all associate with DNA elements in the same regions of the promoters of PID and HEC1.
source: Although only ETT is expected to bind DNA, ChIP followed by qPCR revealed that all three proteins associate with DNA elements in the same regions of the promoters of PID and HEC1 (Figure 5a–c).
evidence: ChIP-qPCR data showing co-localization of all three proteins at target gene promoters.

claim: ETT association with PID and HEC1 promoter regions is largely unaffected by IAA treatment, while TPL and HDA19 interactions are reduced upon auxin treatment.
source: Moreover, while ETT association with these promoter regions was largely unaffected in the presence of IAA, TPL and HDA19 interactions are reduced upon auxin treatment (Figure 5a–c).
evidence: ChIP-qPCR data comparing protein-DNA associations with and without IAA treatment.

claim: H3K27 acetylation increases in the absence of ETT and upon treatment with auxin at PID and HEC1 promoters.
source: H3K27 acetylation increased in the absence of ETT and upon treatment with auxin. This occurred in the same regions of the PID and HEC1 promoters where the proteins were found to associate (Figure 5d,e).
evidence: ChIP data measuring H3K27 acetylation levels in different genetic backgrounds and treatment conditions.

claim: There is no further increase of H3K27 acetylation in the ett-3 mutant upon treatment with auxin.
source: In agreement with ETT mediating the association of TPL/TPR and HDA19 with these regions, there was no further increase of acetylation in the ett-3 mutant upon treatment with auxin (Figure 5d,e).
evidence: ChIP data showing acetylation levels in ett-3 mutant with and without auxin treatment.

claim: Under low auxin conditions, an ETT-TPL-HDA19 complex binds to ETT-target genes keeping their chromatin environments repressed through deacetylation.
source: Under low auxin conditions an ETT-TPL-HDA19 complex binds to ETT-target genes keeping their chromatin environments repressed, through de-acetylation.
evidence: Model synthesized from ChIP, expression, and protein interaction data showing complex formation and chromatin state.

claim: High nuclear auxin concentrations abolish the ETT-TPL-HDA19 complex through direct ETT-auxin interaction, leading to accumulation of histone acetylation and up-regulation of ETT-target genes.
source: High nuclear auxin concentrations abolish the ETT-TPL-HDA19 complex through direct ETT-auxin interaction. This leads to an accumulation of histone acetylation and up-regulation of ETT-target genes.
evidence: Model synthesized from multiple experimental approaches showing auxin-dependent dissociation and gene activation.

claim: The direct binding of auxin allows ETT to switch the chromatin locally between repressive and de-repressive states in an instantly reversible manner.
source: The direct binding of auxin allows ETT to switch the chromatin locally between repressive and de-repressive states. The recent report of ETT negatively regulating STM expression (Chung et al., 2019) provides molecular evidence that ETT can function as a repressor. Whether ETT also has a role in recruiting activating components is yet to be clarified. Indeed, different modes of actions are possible that could depend on other interacting partners or auxin levels and even be target-gene specific. Nevertheless, the effect of auxin on ETT-mediated regulation of the genes studied here is instantly reversible, making it possible to switch between states, immediately responding to changes in auxin levels.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing rapid, reversible changes in chromatin state and gene expression in response to auxin.

claim: The ETT-mediated auxin signaling mechanism is reminiscent of animal hormonal signaling pathways such as the Thyroid Hormone and Wnt/β-catenin pathways.
source: This feature, which is reminiscent of animal hormonal signalling pathways such as the Thyroid Hormone and Wnt/ß-catenin pathways (Tsai and O'Malley, 1994; Gammons and Bienz, 2018), may be particularly important in controlling changes in tissue polarity during plant organogenesis as observed in the Arabidopsis gynoecium (Moubayidin and Ostergaard, 2014).
evidence: Comparison to known animal hormone signaling mechanisms supported by citations.

claim: ETT was shown to recruit HDA19 to the STM promoter, although not via direct protein interaction.
source: Moreover, HDA19 was also recently shown to participate in the repression of STM (Chung et al., 2019). In that study, ETT was shown to recruit HDA19 to the STM promoter, although not via direct protein interaction.
evidence: Citation to previous work (Chung et al., 2019) describing ETT-HDA19 relationship at STM locus.

claim: TPL was originally identified as a key factor involved in setting up the apical-basal growth axis during embryo development.
source: TPL was originally identified as a key factor involved in setting up the apical-basal growth axis during embryo development (Long et al., 2006; Smith and Long, 2010).
evidence: Citation to previous work identifying TPL function in embryo development.

claim: Large-scale interaction studies suggest that the five Arabidopsis TPL/TPRs have roles throughout plant development.
source: Large-scale interaction studies suggest that the five Arabidopsis TPL/TPRs have roles throughout plant development (Krogan et al., 2012; Causier et al., 2012).
evidence: Citation to large-scale studies characterizing TPL/TPR functions.

claim: The most dramatic phenotypes of ett loss-of-function mutants are observed during gynoecium development.
source: Whilst ETT has been implicated in a wide array of developmental processes (Garcia et al., 2006; Marin et al., 2010; Kelley et al., 2012; Pekker et al., 2005), the most dramatic phenotypes of ett loss-of-function mutants are observed during gynoecium development (Sessions et al., 1997; Sessions and Zambryski, 1995; Nemhauser et al., 2000).
evidence: Citations to multiple studies characterizing ett mutant phenotypes.

claim: ETT is highly expressed in the gynoecium.
source: In accordance with this, ETT is highly expressed in the gynoecium (Figure 4a; Simonini et al., 2016).
evidence: GUS reporter expression data and citation to previous expression analysis.

claim: In canonical auxin signalling, auxin-responsive genes are repressed when auxin levels are low by Aux/IAA transcriptional repressors that interact with DNA-bound Auxin Response Factors (ARFs).
source: In canonical auxin signalling, auxin-responsive genes are repressed when auxin levels are low by Aux/IAA transcriptional repressors that interact with DNA-bound Auxin Response Factors (ARFs).
evidence: Description of established canonical auxin signaling mechanism.

claim: As auxin levels increase, the auxin molecule binds to members of the TIR1/AFB family of auxin co-receptors.
source: As auxin levels increase, the auxin molecule binds to members of the TIR1/AFB family of auxin co-receptors (Kepinski and Leyser, 2005; Dharmasiri et al., 2005).
evidence: Description of canonical auxin perception mechanism supported by citations.

claim: The main role of TIR1/AFB auxin perception mechanism is transcriptional reprogramming realized by interaction with Aux/IAA repressors, leading to their ubiquitination and subsequent degradation by the 26S proteasome.
source: The main role of this auxin perception mechanism, besides non-transcriptionally inhibiting growth (Fendrych et al., 2018; Gallei et al., 2019), is transcriptional reprogramming. This is realised by interaction with Aux/IAA repressors, leading to their ubiquitination and subsequent degradation by the 26S proteasome, ultimately relieving the repression of ARF-targeted loci (Kelley and Estelle, 2012; Leyser, 2018; Weijers and Wagner, 2016).
evidence: Description of canonical auxin signaling mechanism supported by multiple citations.

claim: An alternative auxin-signalling mechanism was recently identified whereby auxin directly affects the activity of a transcription factor complex towards its downstream targets.
source: We recently identified an alternative auxin-signalling mechanism whereby auxin directly affects the activity of a transcription factor (TF) complex towards its downstream targets (Simonini et al., 2016; Simonini et al., 2017).
evidence: Citation to previous work by the authors identifying non-canonical auxin signaling.

claim: The alternative auxin-signalling mechanism mediates precise polarity switches during organ initiation and patterning and includes ETTIN (ETT/ARF3) as a pivotal component.
source: This mechanism mediates precise polarity switches during organ initiation and patterning and includes the ARF, ETTIN (ETT/ARF3) as a pivotal component.
evidence: Description of previously identified mechanism from cited work.

claim: EAR motifs are found in Aux/IAA proteins and mediate interactions between Aux/IAA and members of the TOPLESS and TOPLESS-RELATED (TPL/TPR) family of co-repressors.
source: Ethylene-responsive element binding factor-associated Amphiphilic Repression (EAR) motifs are also found in Aux/IAA proteins. Interactions between Aux/IAA and members of the TOPLESS and TOPLESS-RELATED (TPL/TPR) family of co-repressors occur via this motif (Szemenyei et al., 2008).
evidence: Description of known protein interaction mechanism supported by citation.

claim: TPL/TPRs mediate their repressive effect by attracting histone deacetylases (HDACs) to promote chromatin condensation.
source: TPL/TPRs mediate their repressive effect by attracting histone deacetylases (HDACs) to promote chromatin condensation (Krogan et al., 2012).
evidence: Description of known mechanism of TPL/TPR function supported by citation.

claim: ETT is required to keep Histone H3 at a deacetylated state at the gene locus of SHOOT MERISTEMLESS (STM) thereby repressing STM expression.
source: It was recently shown that ETT is required to keep Histone H3 at a deacetylated state at the gene locus of the meristem identity gene SHOOT MERISTEMLESS (STM) thereby repressing STM expression (Chung et al., 2019).
evidence: Citation to recent work characterizing ETT function at STM locus.

claim: TPL was shown previously to recruit histone deacetylase HDA19 during early Arabidopsis flower development to keep chromatin in a repressed state.
source: TPL was shown previously to recruit histone deacetylase, HDA19, during early Arabidopsis flower development to keep chromatin in a repressed state (Krogan et al., 2012).
evidence: Citation to previous work characterizing TPL-HDA19 interaction.

claim: The identification of a direct auxin-ETT interaction to control gene expression adds an additional layer of complexity to auxin action.
source: The identification of a direct auxin-ETT interaction to control gene expression adds an additional layer of complexity to auxin action, which contributes towards explaining how auxin imparts its effect on highly diverse processes throughout plant development.
evidence: Interpretation of the significance of the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: This work opens the possibility that direct transcription factor-ligand interactions is a general feature in the control of gene expression in plants as found in animals.
source: In a broader context, this work also opens for the exciting possibility that direct transcription factor-ligand interactions is a general feature in the control of gene expression in plants as found in animals.
evidence: Speculation about broader implications of the findings.

claim: The concentrations of IAA applied in the DARTS assay (0.1 µM, 1 µM, 10 µM) were selected to saturate the protein with ligand and to ensure maximal protection from proteolysis.
source: The concentrations of IAA applied (0.1 µM, 1 µM, 10 µM) were selected to saturate the protein with ligand and to ensure maximal protection from proteolysis.
evidence: Explanation of experimental design rationale.

claim: Benzoic acid (BA) was applied as a negative control in the DARTS assay because of its similar size and pKa as IAA.
source: As a negative control, benzoic acid (BA) was applied at the same dose as IAA (10 µM and 100 µM) because of its similar size and pKa as IAA.
evidence: Explanation of control selection rationale based on chemical properties.

claim: The region responsible for IAA-sensitivity is situated within the C-terminal part of ETT, known as the ETT-Specific (ES) domain.
source: The region responsible for IAA-sensitivity is situated within the C-terminal part of ETT, known as the ETT-Specific (ES) domain.
evidence: Description based on previous characterization of ETT protein structure and function.

claim: A protein fragment containing 207 amino acids of the ES domain, ES388-594, is sufficient for mediating IAA-sensitivity in ETT-protein interactions.
source: A protein fragment containing 207 amino acids of the ES domain, ES388-594, sufficient for mediating IAA-sensitivity in ETT-protein interactions, was produced recombinantly and shown to be intrinsically disordered (Simonini et al., 2018).
evidence: Citation to previous work characterizing the ES domain fragment.

claim: The ES388-594 protein fragment was shown to be intrinsically disordered.
source: A protein fragment containing 207 amino acids of the ES domain, ES388-594, sufficient for mediating IAA-sensitivity in ETT-protein interactions, was produced recombinantly and shown to be intrinsically disordered (Simonini et al., 2018).
evidence: Citation to previous work characterizing the ES domain fragment structure.

claim: The inability to obtain a Kd value for the ETT-IAA interaction may be due to the interaction being weak as well as potential protein aggregation.
source: We were unable to obtain a Kd value for the interaction, which may be due to the interaction being weak as well as potential protein aggregation.
evidence: Speculation about technical limitations of the ITC experiment.

claim: The ETT-auxin interaction may be stabilized by interacting protein partners in planta that are not present in the in vitro ITC experiment.
source: This could reflect that the ETT-auxin interaction is stabilised by interacting protein partners in planta that are not present in this in vitro experiment.
evidence: Speculation about potential reasons for weak in vitro binding.

claim: Single loss-of-function mutants in TPL and TPR2 do not show any abnormal phenotypes during gynoecium development.
source: Single loss-of-function mutants in TPL and TPR2 do not show any abnormal phenotypes during gynoecium development.
evidence: Phenotypic observation from mutant analysis.

claim: ETT, TPL and TPR2 cooperate to regulate gynoecium development.
source: Together with the protein interaction data and the overlapping expression patterns, these results suggest that ETT and TPL/TPR2 cooperate to regulate gynoecium development.
evidence: Inference from combined expression, interaction, and phenotypic data.

claim: Low levels of auxin maintain ETT associations with TPL/TPR2 to repress gene expression via H3K27 deacetylation.
source: Our data lead to a model in which low levels of auxin maintain ETT associations with TPL/TPR2 to repress gene expression via H3K27 deacetylation.
evidence: Model synthesized from multiple experimental results including ChIP, expression, and interaction data.

claim: As auxin levels increase, TPL/TPR2 (and hence HDA19) disassociate from ETT, promoting H3K27 acetylation.
source: As auxin levels increase, TPL/TPR2 (and hence HDA19) disassociate from ETT, promoting H3K27 acetylation (Figure 5f).
evidence: Model synthesized from ChIP and protein interaction data showing auxin-dependent changes.

claim: The model molecularly underpins the published association between auxin dynamics and PID expression at the gynoecium apex.
source: This model molecularly underpins the published association between auxin dynamics and PID expression at the gynoecium apex where PID is repressed at early stages of development to allow symmetry transition, but subsequently de-repressed as auxin levels rise to facilitate polar auxin transport (Simonini et al., 2016; Moubayidin and Ostergaard, 2014).
evidence: Connection of current findings to previously published developmental observations supported by citations.

claim: It is possible that the effect of auxin on ETT varies depending on the developmental context.
source: Whilst this model explains the data on ETT-mediated auxin signalling during gynoecium development, it is possible that the effect of auxin on ETT varies depending on the developmental context.
evidence: Speculation about potential context-dependent variation in mechanism.

claim: The concentrations of auxin required to mediate its effect on ETT is likely to differ between diverse ETT-containing complexes.
source: Moreover, the concentrations of auxin required to mediate its effect on ETT is likely to differ between diverse ETT-containing complexes.
evidence: Speculation about potential variation in auxin sensitivity across different contexts.

claim: ETT can function as a repressor, as evidenced by its negative regulation of STM expression.
source: The recent report of ETT negatively regulating STM expression (Chung et al., 2019) provides molecular evidence that ETT can function as a repressor.
evidence: Citation to recent work demonstrating ETT repressor function.

claim: Whether ETT also has a role in recruiting activating components is yet to be clarified.
source: Whether ETT also has a role in recruiting activating components is yet to be clarified.
evidence: Acknowledgment of unknown aspects of ETT function.

claim: Different modes of ETT action are possible that could depend on other interacting partners or auxin levels and even be target-gene specific.
source: Indeed, different modes of actions are possible that could depend on other interacting partners or auxin levels and even be target-gene specific.
evidence: Speculation about potential mechanistic diversity.

claim: The instantly reversible nature of ETT-mediated gene regulation may be particularly important in controlling changes in tissue polarity during plant organogenesis.
source: This feature, which is reminiscent of animal hormonal signalling pathways such as the Thyroid Hormone and Wnt/ß-catenin pathways (Tsai and O'Malley, 1994; Gammons and Bienz, 2018), may be particularly important in controlling changes in tissue polarity during plant organogenesis as observed in the Arabidopsis gynoecium (Moubayidin and Ostergaard, 2014).
evidence: Inference about functional significance based on mechanism and previous observations of polarity changes.

claim: Hormonal signalling in animals often involves direct transcription factor-hormone interactions that modulate gene expression.
source: Hormonal signalling in animals often involves direct transcription factor-hormone interactions that modulate gene expression.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about animal hormone signaling.

claim: Plant hormone signalling is most commonly based on de-repression via the degradation of transcriptional repressors.
source: In contrast, plant hormone signalling is most commonly based on de-repression via the degradation of transcriptional repressors.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about plant hormone signaling.

claim: ETTIN directly binds auxin, leading to dissociation from co-repressor proteins of the TOPLESS/TOPLESS-RELATED family followed by histone acetylation and induction of gene expression.
source: Here we show that ETTIN directly binds auxin, leading to dissociation from co-repressor proteins of the TOPLESS/TOPLESS-RELATED family followed by histone acetylation and induction of gene expression.
evidence: Summary of main findings from multiple experimental approaches presented in the manuscript.

claim: The ETT-auxin signaling mechanism is reminiscent of animal hormone signalling as it affects the activity towards regulation of target genes.
source: This mechanism is reminiscent of animal hormone signalling as it affects the activity towards regulation of target genes and provides the first example of a DNA-bound hormone receptor in plants.
evidence: Comparison and interpretation of the significance of the findings.

claim: ETT provides the first example of a DNA-bound hormone receptor in plants.
source: This mechanism is reminiscent of animal hormone signalling as it affects the activity towards regulation of target genes and provides the first example of a DNA-bound hormone receptor in plants.
evidence: Claim about the novelty of the findings in the context of plant biology.

claim: Whilst auxin affects canonical ARFs indirectly by facilitating degradation of Aux/IAA repressors, direct ETTIN-auxin interactions allow switching between repressive and de-repressive chromatin states in an instantly-reversible manner.
source: Whilst auxin affects canonical ARFs indirectly by facilitating degradation of Aux/IAA repressors, direct ETTIN-auxin interactions allow switching between repressive and de-repressive chromatin states in an instantly-reversible manner.
evidence: Comparison of canonical and non-canonical auxin signaling mechanisms based on experimental findings.

claim: Developmental programmes within multicellular organisms originate from a single cell that proliferates into numerous cells ultimately differentiating to make up specialised tissues and organs.
source: Developmental programmes within multicellular organisms originate from a single cell (i.e. a fertilised oocyte) that proliferates into numerous cells ultimately differentiating to make up specialised tissues and organs.
evidence: Statement of general biological knowledge about development.

claim: Tight temporal and spatial regulation of genes involved in developmental processes is essential for proper development of the organism.
source: Tight temporal and spatial regulation of the genes involved in these processes is essential for proper development of the organism.
evidence: Statement of general biological principle.

claim: Changes in gene expression are often controlled by mobile signals that translate positional information into cell type-specific transcriptional outputs.
source: Changes in gene expression are often controlled by mobile signals that translate positional information into cell type-specific transcriptional outputs (Hironaka and Morishita, 2012).
evidence: Statement of general biological principle supported by citation.

claim: In plants, coordination of gene expression can be facilitated by phytohormones such as auxin, which controls processes throughout plant development.
source: In plants, this coordination can be facilitated by phytohormones such as auxin, which controls processes throughout plant development (Vanneste and Friml, 2009).
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about auxin function supported by citation.
